etymology: Latin falsificare, from falsus, false, and facere, to make. In Amos 8:5 the participle falsifying renders the Hebrew 'avath, to bend, make crooked, pervert.
biblical_def: Amos exposes the merchants of Israel who kept the holy days with one eye on the market. “Hear this, O ye that swallow up the needy, even to make the poor of the land to fail” (Amos 8:4). They resented the feasts that stopped trade: “Saying, When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit?” (Amos 8:5). A smaller measure to sell by, a heavier weight to be paid by, and a scale bent to cheat: the falsified balance robbed the poor three ways at once. The law had forbidden it from the beginning, and Proverbs gives God's verdict plainly: “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1). Religious observance that waits impatiently to get back to cheating is no observance at all.

2. To disprove; to prove to be false; as, to falsify a record.
3. To violate; to break by falsehood; as, to falsify one's faith or word.
4. To show to be unsound, insufficient or not proof. [Not in use.] His ample shield is falsified.
FALS'IFY, verb intransitive To tell lies; to violate the truth. It is universally unlawful to lie and falsify

corruption_paragraphs: The word keeps its meaning. What has changed is the instrument: falsified balances now take the form of misleading accounts, hidden fees and manipulated measures, and the sin is the same.

etymology: Middle English plot, a piece of ground, with the sense of scheme influenced by French complot, a conspiracy. In Psalm 37:12 plotteth renders the Hebrew zamam, to devise, purpose, plan evil.
biblical_def: Psalm 37 is David's counsel against fretting at the success of the wicked, and it does not pretend the wicked are harmless. “The wicked plotteth against the just, and gnasheth upon him with his teeth” (Psalm 37:12). The plotting is real and the hatred is real. But the next verse looks from the plotter to heaven: “The Lord shall laugh at him: for he seeth that his day is coming” (Psalm 37:13). The same laughter rings in the second Psalm, over the nations that rage against the LORD and His Anointed: “He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision” (Psalm 2:4). God does not laugh because the plot is trivial; He laughs because its end is already fixed. The righteous may therefore rest in the LORD and wait patiently for Him. The wicked plot; God has numbered their days.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PLOT, noun. Any scheme, stratagem or plan of a complicated nature, or consisting of many parts, adapted to the accomplishment of some purpose, usually a mischievous one.
webster_full: PLOT, noun [a different orthography of plat.] 1. A plat or small extent of ground; as a garden plot It was a chosen plot of fertile land. When we mean to build, We first survey the plot
2. A plantation laid out.
3. A plan or scheme. [Qu. the next word.]
4. In surveying, a plan or draught of a field, farm or manor surveyed and delineated on paper.
PLOT, verb transitive To make a plan of; to delineate.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. The temptation the psalm addresses is perennial: to fret, envy and despair when evil men scheme and seem to prosper.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is rest in God's sovereignty. The believer does not need to match plot with plot; the Lord sees that the plotter's day is coming.

etymology: Latin repetere, to seek again, from re- and petere, to seek, aim at. In Proverbs 17:9 repeateth renders the Hebrew shanah, to do again, to repeat.
biblical_def: Proverbs sets two ways of handling a fault side by side. “He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends” (Proverbs 17:9). To cover is not to excuse sin before God but to refuse to keep broadcasting a wrong that has been dealt with. To repeat is to bring the matter up again and again, to the offender or to others, until the friendship breaks. Solomon had said the same thing earlier: “Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins” (Proverbs 10:12). Peter carries the proverb into the church: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). The repeater may tell only the truth, and still sin, because the purpose of his repeating is not restoration but separation.

webster_full: REPE'AT, verb transitive [Latin repeto; re and peto, to make at or drive towards. this verb ought to be written repete, in analogy with compete, and with repetition.] 1. 2. To try again. I the danger will repeat
3. to recite; to rehearse. He repeated some lines of Virgil. To repeat signals, in the navy, is to make the same signal which the admiral or commander has made, or to make a signal again.
REPE'AT, noun 1. In music, a mark directing a part to be repeated in performance.
2. Repetition.

corruption_summary: Covering a transgression is twisted into concealing abuse and crime, when Scripture means the charity that refuses to rehearse a forgiven fault.
corruption_paragraphs: The proverb has been abused by church leaders to silence victims and hide criminal sin. That is not covering in love; it is complicity, and Scripture requires that crimes be brought to the magistrate (Romans 13:4) and that unrepentant sin be dealt with by church discipline (Matthew 18:15-17).

The opposite error is the culture of endless exposure, where every fault is repeated until reputations and friendships are destroyed. The principle to recover is charity that covers what has been confessed and forgiven, and refuses to keep repeating it.

etymology: From mis-, wrongly, and use, Latin usus. In 2 Chronicles 36:16 misused renders the Hebrew ta'a', to mock, deride, treat with contempt.
biblical_def: The Chronicler's last word on Judah before the exile is a verdict on how the people treated God's messengers. God had been patient: “And the LORD God of their fathers sent to them by his messengers, rising up betimes, and sending; because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place” (2 Chronicles 36:15). They answered compassion with contempt: “But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy” (2 Chronicles 36:16). The word misused means mocked and mistreated. Jeremiah was beaten, imprisoned, thrown into a pit. Christ gathered the whole history into a lament over the city: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee” (Matthew 23:37). To misuse God's messengers is to refuse God, and there comes a point when there is no remedy.

2. To abuse; to treat ill.

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. The Chronicler's theology of judgment is often softened into a story of political misfortune; he insists that the exile came because Judah despised the word of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverence for God's word and for those who faithfully preach it. Patience has a limit, and the limit is called no remedy.

pos: v.t. (to lay on, as a punishment)
etymology: Latin infligere, inflictus, to strike on, from in and fligere, to strike. In 2 Corinthians 2:6 it is supplied by the translators to complete the sense of the Greek epitimia, a penalty, censure.
biblical_def: Paul's second letter to Corinth shows what church discipline is for. A man had been censured by the congregation, and he had repented. “Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many” (2 Corinthians 2:6). The discipline was real, imposed by the church acting together, and it had done its work. Now the church must change course: “So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow” (2 Corinthians 2:7). Paul's plea is direct: “Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him” (2 Corinthians 2:8). A punishment inflicted by the church is never an end in itself. Its aim is repentance and restoration, and when repentance comes, the same body that inflicted the censure must lift it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INFLICT, verb transitive. To lay on; to throw or send on; to apply; as, to inflict pain or disgrace; to inflict punishment on an offender.
webster_full: INFLICT ', verb transitive [Latin inflictus, infligo; in and fligo, to strike;
Eng. to flog.] To lay on; to throw or send on; to apply; as, to inflict pain or disgrace; to inflict punishment on an offender.
To inflict an office, condition, knowledge, tenderness, etc. on one, as used by Chesterfield, is not an authorized use of the word.
The word occurs once in the Authorized Version, at 2 Corinthians 2:6.
There it is used of a censure laid on an offender by the church.

corruption_summary: Church discipline is either abandoned as unloving or practised as punishment with no end, when Paul shows it inflicted by the congregation and lifted on repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: Much of the modern church has given up corrective discipline as harsh and judgmental, leaving open sin uncorrected. Other communities have practised it as permanent shunning. Paul rebukes both: the congregation must act (1 Corinthians 5), and the congregation must forgive and restore the penitent (2 Corinthians 2).

The principle to recover is congregational discipline as the 1689 Confession describes it in chapter 26: exercised by the church for the reclaiming of the offender, and ended with forgiveness and comfort when he repents.

etymology: From hot, Old English hat, plus -ly. In Genesis 31:36 it renders the Hebrew dalaq 'achar, to burn after, to pursue hotly.
biblical_def: Jacob fled from Laban with his wives, children and flocks, and Laban chased him. “And he took his brethren with him, and pursued after him seven days' journey; and they overtook him in the mount Gilead” (Genesis 31:23). When Laban searched the tents and found nothing, Jacob's twenty years of grievance broke out: “And Jacob was wroth, and chode with Laban: and Jacob answered and said to Laban, What is my trespass? what is my sin, that thou hast so hotly pursued after me?” (Genesis 31:36). The Hebrew pictures a fire burning behind him. Jacob lists his years of service and Laban's changing of his wages, and then gives God the credit for his survival: “Except the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely thou hadst sent me away now empty” (Genesis 31:42). Laban pursued hotly; God had gone before and warned him in a dream not to harm Jacob.

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. The Jacob narratives are sometimes read as folklore about a trickster; Scripture presents them as the history of the patriarch through whom the covenant line ran, and shows God's faithfulness to a flawed man.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's protection of His people under pursuit. The God of Abraham and the fear of Isaac stood between Jacob and the man who hotly pursued him.

pos: v.t. (to write down as a rule; to lay down authoritatively)
etymology: Latin praescribere, to write before, to order, from prae and scribere, to write. In Isaiah 10:1 prescribed renders the Hebrew kathab, to write.
biblical_def: Isaiah's woe falls on lawmakers. “Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed” (Isaiah 10:1). The wrong is done with a pen, through statutes duly prescribed. The purpose of the laws is named: “To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and that they may rob the fatherless!” (Isaiah 10:2). Legality is not righteousness. A law can be properly written, formally enacted and wicked, and God holds its makers accountable. The prophet's question follows: “And what will ye do in the day of visitation, and in the desolation which shall come from far? to whom will ye flee for help? and where will ye leave your glory?” (Isaiah 10:3). The lawgiver who prescribes oppression will stand before the Lawgiver who prescribed justice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PRESCRI'BE, verb transitive [Latin proescribo, to write before.] 1. In medicine, to direct, as a remedy to be used or applied to a diseased patient. Be not offended with the physician who prescribes harsh remedies.
webster_full: PRESCRI'BE, verb transitive [Latin proescribo, to write before.] 1. In medicine, to direct, as a remedy to be used or applied to a diseased patient. Be not offended with the physician who prescribes harsh remedies.
2. To set or lay down authoritatively for direction; to give as a rule of conduct; as, to prescribe laws or rules. There's joy, when to wild will you laws prescribe
3. To direct. Let streams prescribe their fountains where to run.
PRESCRI'BE, verb intransitive To write or give medical directions; to direct what remedies are to be used; as, to prescribe for a patient in a fever.
1. To give law; to influence arbitrarily. A forwardness to prescribe to the opinions of others.

corruption_summary: Positive law is treated as its own justification, as if what is legally prescribed must be right, when Isaiah pronounces woe on unrighteous decrees.
corruption_paragraphs: Legal positivism, the doctrine that law is simply what the governing authority enacts, with no higher standard, dominates modern jurisprudence. Isaiah stands with the whole Reformed tradition of natural and revealed law: rulers are ministers of God (Romans 13:4), their laws are measured by His, and a decree that preys on the widow and the fatherless is an unrighteous decree however duly it was enacted.
The principle to recover is the lordship of Christ over every sphere, including the legislature. Magistrates prescribe under God, and will answer to Him in the day of visitation.

pos: n. (one of the sides in a cause at law)
etymology: Old French partie, a part, a side, from Latin partiri, to divide. In Exodus 22:9 both parties renders the Hebrew shenehem, the two of them.
biblical_def: The law of Moses gave every disputed claim a hearing. “For all manner of trespass, whether it be for ox, for ass, for sheep, for raiment, or for any manner of lost thing, which another challengeth to be his, the cause of both parties shall come before the judges; and whom the judges shall condemn, he shall pay double unto his neighbour” (Exodus 22:9). Both parties are heard, and the judges decide. Webster cites the verse for party as one of two litigants. The judges themselves are bound: “Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God's” (Deuteronomy 1:17). And Proverbs supplies the reason both must be heard: “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Proverbs 18:17). The first story always sounds right until the other party speaks.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): P'ARTY, noun [Latin pars. See Part.] 1. A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community. It differs from faction, in implying a less dishonorable association, or more justifiable designs.
webster_full: P'ARTY, noun [Latin pars. See Part.] 1. A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community. It differs from faction, in implying a less dishonorable association, or more justifiable designs. Parties exist in all governments;
2. One of two litigants; the plaintiff or defendant in a lawsuit. The cause of both parties shall come before the judges. Exodus 22:1.
3. One concerned or interested in an affair. This man was not a party to the trespass or affray. He is not a party to the contract or agreement.
4. Side; persons engaged against each other. The peace both parties want, is like to last. Small parties make up in diligence what they want in numbers.
5. Cause; side. Aegle came in to make their party good.

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. The principle it carries, that both parties must be heard before judgment, is under pressure wherever accusation is treated as proof and the accused is condemned by the crowd before any hearing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is due process as God's law gives it: two or three witnesses, both parties heard, no respect of persons, because the judgment is God's.

etymology: Old French gai, merry, bright, perhaps of Germanic origin. In James 2:3 it renders the Greek lampros, bright, splendid, magnificent.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version gay means showy, and James uses it to expose partiality in the church. “My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons” (James 2:1). He paints the scene: “For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment” (James 2:2). The ushers know what to do: “And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool” (James 2:3). The gay clothing is the rich man's splendid robe, and the church that seats by wardrobe has forgotten the Lord of glory, who became poor. Webster (1828) gives the same sense: fine, showy, as a gay dress.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): GAY, adjective 1. Merry; airy; jovial; sportive; frolicksome.
webster_full: GAY, adjective 1. Merry; airy; jovial; sportive; frolicksome.
It denotes more life and animation than cheerful.
Belinda smiled, and all the world was gay
2. Fine; showy; as a gay dress.
3. Inflamed or merry with liquor; intoxicated; a vulgar use of the word in America.

corruption_summary: The word has been taken over as the name of a sexual identity, and the KJV's plain meaning is now heard as something it never said.
corruption_paragraphs: Within the twentieth century gay passed from meaning merry or showy to naming homosexual desire, and then a self-chosen identity built on it. Readers of James 2:3 now hear the verse wrongly, and some have mocked the Authorized Version for it. The text has not changed; the language around it has. The dictionary holds Scripture's teaching that marriage is one man and one woman, and that every sexual union outside it is sin from which Christ calls sinners to repentance and cleansing (1 Corinthians 6:9-11).

The principle to recover is twofold: to read the KJV in its own English, where gay clothing is splendid dress, and to refuse to let any desire become the definition of a person made in the image of God. James's warning also stands: the church must not seat men by their clothes, rich or poor.

etymology: From late, Old English laet, plus -ly. In Acts 18:2 it renders the Greek prosphatos, freshly, recently.
biblical_def: Paul arrived in Corinth alone and found a couple who would become two of his dearest helpers. “And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them” (Acts 18:2). They were refugees, lately expelled by an emperor's edict, and Roman historians confirm Claudius' expulsion of the Jews around AD 49. Paul joined them in their trade: “And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Acts 18:3). An imperial decree uprooted a household, and God planted it beside the apostle. Years later Paul could write: “Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus” (Romans 16:3). Their recent displacement was God's placement.

webster_full: LA'TELY, adverb Not long ago; recently.

There it renders the Greek prosphatos, recently.
Aquila and Priscilla had lately come from Italy after Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. Luke's note about Claudius is one of many points where Acts is confirmed by Roman sources, in this case Suetonius.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is providence in displacement. Aquila and Priscilla were lately come from Italy because they were driven out, and God used it to give Paul fellow workers.
roots_summary: Late plus -ly; rendering Greek prosphatos, recently, at Acts 18:2.
roots_lines: Old English laet, late, slow.
Greek prosphatos, fresh, recent.
Acts 18:2 says Aquila was lately come from Italy.
Acts 18:3 records Paul working with them as a tentmaker.
Romans 16:3 calls Priscilla and Aquila Paul's helpers in Christ.
